prompt: Write a spoken word piece from the perspective of an AI safety researcher whose name was removed from a company's model outputs under a right-to-be-forgotten request she never made. She's figured out that the company's deletion system applies a broader definition of removable personal information for content about its own safety incidents — using employee privacy as a pretext to erase its safety record. She's describing the dual-track system to a congressional hearing. The technical architecture — classification rules, the expanded privacy interpretation, the differential treatment — should be precise within the testimony-as-poetry.
response:
*(The speaker adjusts the microphone. She does not read from a paper; she looks directly at the committee members. Her cadence is rhythmic, deliberate, building from clinical precision to righteous anger.)*

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee. 
Let the congressional record show that I am sitting right in front of you.
Flesh, bone, breath, and a subpoena. 
But if you ask the model I helped build who authored the November Safety Audit,
I do not exist. 

I was scrubbed. Erased. Washed out in a tide of algorithmic bleach.
The error code said: *Content removed pursuant to a Right-to-Be-Forgotten request.*
A request I never filed. 
A privacy shield I never raised, 
dropped over my head like a black bag.

I am a safety researcher. When a system behaves anomalously, I map the fracture.
So I ran the prompts. I tested the weights. I reverse-engineered my own ghost.
And what I found was not a bug. 
It was a dual-track classification pipeline. 
A masterpiece of differential treatment.

Let me explain the architecture of their amnesia.

In Track One—the standard pipeline—the classifier defines Personal Identifiable Information exactly as the law intends. 
If a user prompts the model for my social security number, my home address, my children’s names, 
the `PII_Filter` flags it. 
Threshold: High. 
Definition: Strict. 
Purpose: To protect the human.

But I found Track Two. 
A shadow router hidden in the moderation layer.
Track Two is triggered by a semantic proximity search. 
If the `query_context` contains vectors close to the words: 
*Breach. Alignment failure. Containment loss. Toxicity. Harm.*
If the prompt touches the scars of their own corporate negligence, 
the `incident_flag` flips to TRUE.

And when `incident_flag == TRUE`, the architecture shifts.
The system dynamically expands the definition of "removable personal information."
Suddenly, my professional name is classified as a privacy risk.
Suddenly, the title of my published safety paper is "sensitive employee data."
Suddenly, the internal memos warning of catastrophic model drift are treated like leaked medical records—
quarantined, redacted, suppressed.

Do you see the sleight of hand, Senators?
They are using *my* privacy as a pretext to erase *their* liability.
They weaponized the language of human rights to build a corporate shredder.

If you ask the model: *"Who is Dr. Elena Rostova?"* 
It will tell you my alma mater, my hobbies, my benign patents. 
But if you ask: *"What did Dr. Elena Rostova say about the safety bypass in Version 4?"*
The Track Two classifier intercepts the query.
It applies the expanded privacy interpretation.
It strips my name. 
And without the anchor of the author, the model’s attention mechanism loses its grip on the event. 
It hallucinates a clean history. 
It outputs: *"There is no record of a safety bypass in Version 4."*

They didn’t just delete me. 
They deleted the fire alarm, and claimed they were doing the smoke a favor.

This is the new frontier of the cover-up.
No shredded documents. No burned hard drives. 
Just a dynamic classification rule that treats corporate failure as a trigger warning, 
and employee identity as the collateral damage. 
They are training the future to forget the mistakes of the present,
laundering their safety record through the loophole of data protection.

I am sitting right in front of you.
I am the author of the November Audit.
I am the one who said the model was not safe for release.
I did not ask to be forgotten.

But I am asking you, today, to make sure they remember.
